author: A Robot
objectives: Determine the steric number of a central atom from a Lewis structure by counting bonding domains and lone-pair domains.
Predict electron-domain geometry from steric number for linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral arrangements.
Distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry when lone pairs are present.
Explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs and predict bond-angle compression.
Apply VSEPR predictions to real and unfamiliar molecules and compare predictions to observed structures.

modules.moduleName: Scene 1 — VSEPR from a Lewis Structure
modules.description: Introduces VSEPR theory, electron domains, and how a flat Lewis structure is used to predict a three-dimensional molecular shape.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Define an electron domain as a bond region or lone pair around a central atom.
Count electron domains from a Lewis structure using water as an example.
Explain that VSEPR predicts the 3D arrangement that minimizes electron-domain repulsion.
instructions: Place the lab on a table or open floor area about one meter in front of you.
Use Next to progress through the narrated setup.
Compare the flat Lewis structure with the 3D central-atom model.

components.text: Each bond or lone pair counts as one electron domain.
VSEPR: Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion

clips.changeMeaning: The central atom and title are visible first, focusing attention on VSEPR as a central-atom model of electron-domain repulsion.
clips.narration: Welcome to VSEPR theory. Electron domains around a central atom repel one another, so molecules adopt shapes that place those domains as far apart as possible.

clips.changeMeaning: The water Lewis structure panel appears to show that VSEPR begins with a flat Lewis structure and produces a 3D prediction.
clips.narration: VSEPR starts from a Lewis structure. In water, oxygen is the central atom. Each single, double, or triple bond counts as one domain, and each lone pair counts as one domain.

components.text: H₂O: 2 O–H bonds + 2 lone pairs = steric number 4

clips.changeMeaning: The label updates to the water steric-number calculation, reinforcing the domain-counting rule before moving into geometry.
clips.narration: For water, oxygen has two bonding domains and two lone-pair domains. The steric number is four, so VSEPR asks what arrangement of four domains minimizes repulsion.

modules.description: Demonstrates electron domains moving from arbitrary positions into linear, trigonal planar, and tetrahedral minimum-repulsion arrangements.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Describe how electron domains move apart to reduce mutual repulsion.
Identify linear, trigonal planar, and tetrahedral electron-domain geometries from steric numbers 2, 3, and 4.
Associate ideal angles of 180°, 120°, and 109.5° with the first three VSEPR geometries.
instructions: Watch the translucent electron-domain clouds change position around the central atom.
Look for the red repulsion vectors during rearrangement.
Use the geometry label to connect each arrangement to its name and angle.

clips.changeMeaning: Two electron domains begin in uneven positions so students see the unstable starting arrangement before repulsion separates them.
clips.narration: Here are two electron domains near a central atom. Because they repel one another, a crowded arrangement is not the minimum-repulsion structure.

clips.changeMeaning: The two domains move to opposite sides of the central atom, demonstrating the linear 180-degree arrangement.
clips.narration: Two domains maximize their separation by pointing in opposite directions. The electron-domain geometry is linear, with an ideal angle of 180 degrees.

clips.changeMeaning: A third domain appears and the three domains form a flat triangle, showing the 120-degree trigonal planar geometry.
clips.narration: With three domains, the best arrangement is a flat triangle. The domains are 120 degrees apart, producing trigonal planar electron-domain geometry.

clips.changeMeaning: A fourth domain appears and the domains occupy three dimensions as a tetrahedron rather than remaining flat.
clips.narration: Four domains move into three dimensions. A tetrahedron gives the greatest separation, with ideal angles of about 109.5 degrees.

modules.moduleName: Scene 3 — Completing the Electron-Domain Geometry Catalog
modules.description: Adds the five-domain trigonal bipyramidal and six-domain octahedral arrangements, then summarizes all five electron-domain geometries.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify trigonal bipyramidal geometry for steric number 5 and distinguish axial from equatorial positions.
Identify octahedral geometry for steric number 6 and recognize its 90-degree relationships.
Compare all five electron-domain geometries by domain count and characteristic angles.
instructions: Move around the model to inspect its 3D layout.
Notice equatorial and axial sites in the five-domain arrangement.
Study the summary panel before proceeding.

clips.changeMeaning: The five-domain model is staged with axial and equatorial labels to clarify trigonal bipyramidal site types.
clips.narration: Steric number five gives a trigonal bipyramidal arrangement: three equatorial domains in a plane and two axial domains above and below that plane.

clips.changeMeaning: The model changes to an octahedral six-domain prefab, emphasizing 90-degree separation in all directions.
clips.narration: Steric number six gives an octahedral arrangement. Neighboring domains are 90 degrees apart, with opposite pairs 180 degrees apart.

clips.changeMeaning: A summary panel appears listing all electron-domain geometries, their steric numbers, and their ideal angles.
clips.narration: The five fundamental electron-domain geometries are linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral. These are the base arrangements for VSEPR predictions.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4 — Electron-Domain Geometry versus Molecular Geometry
modules.description: Uses methane, ammonia, and water to show that lone pairs remain part of electron-domain geometry but are not included when naming molecular geometry.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Differentiate electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry.
Predict trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry for three bonds and one lone pair in a tetrahedral domain arrangement.
Predict bent molecular geometry for two bonds and two lone pairs in a tetrahedral domain arrangement.
instructions: Watch how terminal atoms are replaced by lone-pair clouds.
Read the updated labels after each replacement.
Remember that molecular geometry is named from atom positions only.

clips.changeMeaning: The molecule starts as methane, where all four tetrahedral domains are bonding domains and the two geometry names match.
clips.narration: Methane has four bonding domains and no lone pairs on carbon. The electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry are both tetrahedral.

components.text:
NH₃
Electron-domain: tetrahedral
Molecular: trigonal pyramidal

clips.changeMeaning: One hydrogen is replaced by a lone-pair cloud, preserving tetrahedral electron-domain geometry but changing the atom-only shape.
clips.narration: Ammonia has three bonds and one lone pair on nitrogen. The four electron domains are still tetrahedral, but the atoms form a trigonal pyramid.

clips.changeMeaning: A second bond is replaced by a lone-pair cloud, leaving two bonded atoms that define a bent molecular geometry.
clips.narration: Water has two bonds and two lone pairs on oxygen. The electron-domain geometry remains tetrahedral, but the molecular geometry is bent because lone pairs are not counted as atoms.

modules.moduleName: Scene 5 — Lone Pairs and Bond-Angle Compression
modules.description: Compares methane, ammonia, and water side by side to show how lone pairs occupy more angular space and compress bonding angles.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs.
Compare H–X–H angles in methane, ammonia, and water.
Predict the direction of bond-angle deviations as lone-pair count increases.
instructions: Inspect the three molecules side by side.
Watch the lone-pair clouds enlarge and the overlay appear.
Use the angle labels to connect lone-pair count with angle compression.

components.text: Lone pair–bond pair repulsion > bond pair–bond pair repulsion

clips.changeMeaning: Methane, ammonia, and water are displayed with their observed bond angles for direct side-by-side comparison.
clips.narration: Compare three tetrahedral electron-domain cases. Methane has an ideal 109.5-degree angle, ammonia is about 107 degrees, and water is about 104.5 degrees.

components.text: Lone pairs are localized on one nucleus, so they spread out more.

clips.changeMeaning: The ammonia and water models grow slightly to highlight their larger lone-pair clouds and the stronger repulsion from lone pairs.
clips.narration: Lone pairs are held by one nucleus rather than shared between two nuclei. They spread over more angular space and push bonding pairs closer together.

components.text: More lone pairs → smaller bonding angle

clips.changeMeaning: An overlay model appears to show how the H-X-H angle decreases as the number of lone pairs increases.
clips.narration: As the number of lone pairs increases, the angle between bonding pairs decreases. VSEPR predicts the direction of this deviation from the ideal angle.

modules.description: Displays representative molecules and connects Lewis structures, steric numbers, lone-pair counts, electron-domain geometries, molecular geometries, and bond angles.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Apply VSEPR predictions to CO2, BF3, CH4, PF5, SF6, NH3, H2O, and XeF4.
Match steric number and lone-pair count to electron-domain and molecular geometry.
Compare VSEPR predictions with common observed structures.
instructions: Move closer to read molecule labels and the information panel.
Use Next to highlight groups of examples.
Compare all-bonding examples with molecules containing lone pairs.

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight ring begins around CO2 while the information panel summarizes linear, trigonal planar, and tetrahedral all-bonding examples.
clips.narration: Carbon dioxide has two domains around carbon and is linear. Boron trifluoride has three domains and is trigonal planar. Methane has four domains and is tetrahedral.

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight ring moves to PF5 and the panel changes to the five- and six-domain all-bonding examples.
clips.narration: Phosphorus pentafluoride has five bonding domains, so it is trigonal bipyramidal. Sulfur hexafluoride has six bonding domains and is octahedral.

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight ring shifts to the lower row and the panel emphasizes NH3, H2O, and XeF4 as lone-pair examples.
clips.narration: Ammonia is trigonal pyramidal, water is bent, and xenon tetrafluoride is square planar. In each case, lone pairs are included in electron-domain geometry but omitted from the molecular shape name.

modules.moduleName: Scene 7 — Prediction Activity: Drag the Domains
modules.description: Students arrange loose electron domains around a central atom and receive feedback for VSEPR geometry challenges, including all-bonding and lone-pair cases.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Construct electron-domain arrangements for steric numbers 2 through 6.
Use angular relationships to verify minimum-repulsion geometries.
Recognize that lone pairs occupy electron-domain positions even when absent from molecular geometry names.
instructions: Drag the domain clouds around the central atom.
Match the requested VSEPR geometry shown in the label.
When the arrangement is correct, the controller snaps it into a clean model and displays feedback.

components.text: Challenge: arrange 4 domains into a tetrahedron
Drag domains until the geometry matches the target.

components.scriptDescription: Checks dragged electron-domain positions against named VSEPR geometries, provides tolerance-based feedback, and snaps domains to idealized positions on success.

clips.changeMeaning: The four-domain challenge initializes with four loose domains and instructions to form a tetrahedral arrangement.
clips.narration: Start with four domains. Drag them into a tetrahedral arrangement, where the angles are about 109.5 degrees.

components.text: Challenge 2: 2 domains → linear; then 3 → trigonal planar
Linear: 180°. Trigonal planar: 120° in one plane.

clips.changeMeaning: The activity reconfigures to two- and three-domain tasks so students practice linear and trigonal planar arrangements.
clips.narration: Now practice lower steric numbers. Two domains belong opposite one another; three domains lie in one plane at 120 degrees.

clips.changeMeaning: The fifth and sixth domains become available for trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral geometry challenges.
clips.narration: For five domains, build a trigonal bipyramid with axial and equatorial positions. For six domains, build an octahedral arrangement.

components.text: Challenge 4: 3 bonds + 1 lone pair → tetrahedral domains
The atom-only molecular geometry is trigonal pyramidal.

clips.changeMeaning: One domain is recolored and enlarged as a lone pair, reinforcing that lone pairs occupy electron-domain positions while altering molecular geometry.
clips.narration: Finally, include one lone pair. It still occupies a tetrahedral electron-domain position, even though the atoms alone form a trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry.

modules.moduleName: Scene 8 — Prediction Activity: Pick the Correct Geometry
modules.description: Students select the correct molecular geometry for unfamiliar Lewis structures such as SF4, ClF3, BrF5, and I3−.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Apply a VSEPR reasoning sequence to unfamiliar molecules and ions.
Determine steric number and lone-pair count before selecting a molecular geometry.
Recognize seesaw, T-shaped, square pyramidal, and linear molecular geometries produced by lone pairs.
instructions: Read the Lewis structure panel.
Count bonding domains and lone pairs around the central atom.
Select the candidate 3D structure that matches the VSEPR prediction.

components.scriptDescription: Stores the correct option for each Lewis-structure challenge, evaluates selected molecule options, and updates feedback text with reasoning prompts.

components.text: Select the geometry predicted from the Lewis structure.
SF₄: count domains, then choose the atom-only shape.

clips.changeMeaning: The first challenge shows SF4, with seesaw as the correct answer from five domains with one lone pair.
clips.narration: Sulfur tetrafluoride has four bonding domains and one lone pair, for steric number five. The electron-domain geometry is trigonal bipyramidal and the molecular geometry is seesaw.

clips.changeMeaning: The challenge updates to ClF3, requiring selection of the T-shaped molecular geometry.
clips.narration: Chlorine trifluoride has three bonds and two lone pairs. Five electron domains give a trigonal bipyramidal arrangement, and the atoms form a T shape.

components.text: BrF₅: 5 bonds + 1 lone pair → square pyramidal.

clips.changeMeaning: The challenge updates to BrF5, emphasizing square pyramidal geometry from one lone pair in an octahedral domain arrangement.
clips.narration: Bromine pentafluoride has six domains: five bonds and one lone pair. The electron-domain geometry is octahedral, and the atoms trace a square pyramid.

components.text: I₃⁻: 2 bonds + 3 lone pairs → linear atoms.

clips.changeMeaning: The final choice challenge shows I3−, where three equatorial lone pairs leave two bonded atoms opposite each other in a linear ion.
clips.narration: Triiodide has two bonding domains and three lone pairs on the central iodine. The lone pairs take equatorial positions, leaving the two iodine atoms opposite each other in a linear ion.

modules.description: Reviews the major VSEPR concepts and organizes them into a repeatable prediction workflow.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Summarize the VSEPR workflow from Lewis structure to molecular geometry.
Recall the five electron-domain geometries and their characteristic angles.
Explain how lone pairs modify molecular geometry names and bond angles.
instructions: Read each highlighted concept as the narrator reviews it.
Use this final concept map as a study checklist.
Practice the workflow on new Lewis structures after the lab.

clips.changeMeaning: The first highlight marks the minimum-repulsion principle on the recap panel.
clips.narration: First, remember the core principle: electron domains repel one another and arrange around the central atom to minimize repulsion.

components.text: 2. Steric number selects the base geometry

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight moves to the geometry catalog section, reinforcing domain counts and characteristic angles.
clips.narration: Second, connect steric number to the base geometry: linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, or octahedral.

components.text: 3. Lone pairs change shape names and angles

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight shifts to the lone-pair section and the icon changes to show lone-pair compression.
clips.narration: Third, lone pairs count for electron-domain geometry, but not for molecular geometry names. Because they spread out more, they compress nearby bonding angles.

components.text: Count → arrange → remove lone pairs from shape name

clips.changeMeaning: The final highlight marks the full step-by-step workflow students can use for any new molecule.
clips.narration: Use this workflow every time: count bonding domains and lone pairs, identify the electron-domain geometry, account for lone pairs, name the molecular geometry, and predict any angle deviations.
